section.title: Praise the LORD, for He Is Good
section.sectionRationale: A hymn of praise opening Book V's second great block of temple songs, paired liturgically with Psalm 136, weaving creation, the exodus, and the conquest into one call to bless the LORD who chose Jacob and stands utterly above the lifeless idols of the nations.
section.thesis: The LORD alone deserves praise because He is sovereign over creation and history, chose Israel as His treasured possession, and acts, unlike the silent, sightless idols of the nations, so that every house of His people should bless His enduring name.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the call to praise in the temple courts (vv1-4), the LORD's sovereignty over creation and history recalled (vv5-14), the folly of lifeless idols (vv15-18), and a closing chorus of blessing from every house of Israel (vv19-21).

units.label: Praise the name of the LORD
units.note: call to praise in the temple courts

verses.text: Hallelujah! Praise the name of the LORD. Give praise, O servants of the LORD,
who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God.
Hallelujah, for the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely.
For the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, Israel as His {{segullah|treasured possession}}.

units.label: The LORD does all that pleases Him

verses.text: For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods.
The LORD does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths.
He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses.
He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast.
He sent signs and wonders into your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.
He struck down many nations and slaughtered mighty kings:
Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan.
He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel.
Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations.
For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants.
The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men.
They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see;
they have ears, but cannot hear; nor is there breath in their mouths.
Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them.
O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD;
O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!
Blessed be the LORD from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem. Hallelujah!

segullah.gloss: A treasured possession, private property especially valued by its owner. God calls Israel His segullah, echoing Exodus 19:5, a term of intimate, chosen belonging rather than mere ownership.

basic.context: A post exilic hymn calling the priests and Levites standing in the temple courts to praise the LORD, recounting His mastery over creation, His mighty acts in the exodus and conquest, and contrasting His living power with the silent idols of the nations.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes Israel's specific redemptive history as grounds for praise, and by that pattern calls every generation to root worship not in vague sentiment but in concrete acts of God, remembered and retold.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is called God's segullah, a treasured possession, echoing Exodus 19:5. The idols, by contrast, are elilim, worthless things, mere silver and gold shaped by human hands, utterly unlike the LORD who speaks, sees, hears, and acts.
basic.typology: The exodus deliverance and conquest of Canaan's kings foreshadow the greater deliverance and inheritance won in Christ, who defeats every hostile power and gives His people an eternal inheritance, Colossians 2:15, 1 Peter 1:4.
basic.christ: Christ is the true and living Word, unlike the mute idols of verses 16-17; He speaks, sees, hears, and acts decisively in the greater exodus of the cross and resurrection, disarming rulers and authorities, Colossians 2:15, and He is the name that endures forever, Philippians 2:9-11.
basic.god: God is shown as sovereign over nature, active in history's decisive acts of judgment and deliverance, compassionate toward His servants, and utterly incomparable to anything made by human hands.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 19:5 calls Israel God's treasured possession. Jeremiah 10:3-5 mocks idols in nearly identical language. Colossians 2:15 shows Christ disarming rulers and authorities in a greater exodus victory. Revelation 19:1-6 picks up this psalm's Hallelujah chorus in heavenly worship.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's praise for the LORD who chose Israel, ruled creation, and defeated her enemies while idols stood silent, finds its fulfillment in Christ, the living Word who defeats every hostile power and gathers a people, from every nation, as God's own treasured possession.

context.literary:
Psalm 135 is built like a set of nesting boxes, and the middle box is a single verse. It opens and closes with 'Hallelujah,' verses 1 and 21, and the call to praise comes back at the very end in widened form. At the centre sits verse 13, 'Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations,' the only verse addressed directly to God. Everything before it is argued toward that statement, and everything after it unfolds what that enduring name means for the people who carry it.

The movement goes in four steps. Verses 1 to 4 call the temple servants to praise and give the reasons, God's goodness and His choice of Jacob. Verses 5 to 12 move outward, from creation, the clouds, the lightning and the wind in verses 6 and 7, to history, the firstborn of Egypt and the kings of Canaan in verses 8 to 12. Verses 13 and 14 pivot on God's name and His care of His servants. Verses 15 to 18 then turn on the idols with a long list of what they lack, and verses 19 to 21 gather four groups, 'house of Israel,' 'house of Aaron,' 'house of Levi,' and 'you who fear the LORD,' to bless Him from Zion.

There is a clear contrast in the structure. The LORD 'does all that pleases Him,' verse 6, with a string of active verbs: causes, generates, brings forth, struck down, sent, gave. The idols are described by a list of body parts that do not work, mouths, eyes, ears, verses 16 and 17, and by a verb that never applies to them, 'become like them,' verse 18. The poem sets one God who acts against many gods who cannot. A subtler shift is the word 'I' in verse 5, 'I know that the LORD is great,' the only personal voice in the psalm, which makes the whole piece a testimony before it is a lecture.
context.historical:
Psalm 135 has no title and no named author, and it is stitched out of older Scripture. Verse 7 is almost word for word Jeremiah 10:13 and Jeremiah 51:16. Verses 15 to 18 repeat Psalm 115:4-8 with small changes. Verse 14 takes its two main verbs from Deuteronomy 32:36, and verses 19 and 20 lengthen the pattern of Psalm 115:9-12 and Psalm 118:2-4. The psalmist is a person who knows the Law, the Prophets and the earlier hymns by heart and lets them speak. That is why a date is hard to fix, and why many scholars place it late in Israel's history, after the exile, while others see no reason to rule out earlier use.

The setting is the temple. The servants of the LORD 'stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God,' verse 2, and the closing call is to 'bless the LORD from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem,' verse 21. This is a liturgy for a congregation gathered in the courts. If it comes from the period after the exile, as the language and borrowing suggest, then it speaks to a small community who had lost a kingdom and rebuilt a smaller temple, among nations whose gods looked impressive. Nehemiah 9:9-11 does the same, retelling the exodus before the returned community, and includes a line that suits verse 13, 'You made a name for Yourself that endures to this day.'

The history in verses 8 to 12 is selective and ordered. The ten plagues are compressed into the single stroke on the firstborn, Exodus 12:29, and the 'signs and wonders' of Exodus, Deuteronomy 6:22, are directed at Egypt by name in the second person, 'into your midst, O Egypt,' verse 9. The two kings named, Sihon and Og, were the first victories east of the Jordan, Numbers 21:21-35, and they stand for the whole conquest, 'all the kings of Canaan.' The first hearers would have felt these names as the foundation stones of their own right to the land, and as a reminder that the land was given and not seized, verse 12.
context.canonical:
Psalm 135 is a patchwork on purpose, and that makes it one of the clearest examples of Scripture reading Scripture. The line in verse 7 about the clouds rising from the ends of the earth appears in Jeremiah 10:13, in the middle of a prophetic mockery of idols. The mockery of the idols themselves in verses 15 to 18 comes from Psalm 115:4-8, and Isaiah 44:9-20 expands the same point into a sustained satire on the craftsman who burns half the tree and bows down to the rest. Habakkuk 2:18-19 adds that there is 'no breath in it at all,' which is the point of Psalm 135:17.

The psalm sits in a deliberate sequence. It follows Psalm 134, which ends with a blessing from Zion, and picks up the same words in verse 21. It leads into Psalm 136, which retells the same events, creation, the exodus, the defeat of Sihon and Og, with a refrain after every line. In the Psalter's last book the two form a pair, one giving the argument and the other the congregation's response. Psalm 78, Psalm 105, Psalm 106 and Nehemiah 9 also retell Israel's story, but Psalm 135 does so in the form of praise rather than confession.

The New Testament uses verse 14 directly. The footnote to the verse in the BSB notes that the Hebrew can read 'will judge His people,' and that Hebrews 10:30 quotes the parallel in Deuteronomy 32:36 in exactly that form, 'The Lord will judge His people.' The writer to the Hebrews uses it as a warning that the God who defends His people also holds them to account, Hebrews 10:31. Paul's description of idolatry in Romans 1:23-25, where people exchange God's glory for images and 'worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator,' reads like a commentary on verses 15 to 18. The cry of 'Hallelujah' that frames Psalm 135 recurs in Revelation 19:1-6, where a multitude in heaven praises God for His judgments.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist writes to a community that is tempted to look at the world's idols and be impressed. The nations have gold, armies, buildings and craftsmen. The psalmist's answer is not to deny the splendour but to describe what the splendour is: 'silver and gold, made by the hands of men,' verse 15. The intention is to restore proportion. Israel is to remember that its God made the weather, humbled Pharaoh, and gave a land to a people who had no army worth speaking of, and therefore the people should worship with their whole mouth rather than with a sceptical half.

There is also a pastoral aim. The warning of verse 18, 'Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them,' tells the reader that worship shapes the worshiper. A person who gives their trust to something deaf and blind will in time become deaf and blind. The reverse is true too, and the psalm is written so that those who bless the LORD, the God who speaks and sees and hears, would grow like Him in attentiveness. The author wants worship to be the means by which God's people stay alive to Him, and so the poem ends not with an argument but with a roll call of those who are to bless.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The recital of the exodus and conquest in verses 8 to 12 is description. It records what the LORD did to Egypt and to the kings of Canaan, and it does not instruct the reader to strike down anyone. Those verses belong to a particular moment in redemptive history, when God gave a particular land to a particular people and judged particular nations, and the Bible itself treats that moment as unrepeatable. The New Testament never uses the conquest as a model for what the church does to its neighbours.

What the psalm does prescribe is the response. Praise is commanded in verses 1, 3, 19, 20 and 21, with the reasons set out so that praise is not blind. The satire of idols is also an instruction, since it tells hearers what to refuse: any object, ideology or ambition made by human hands that asks for the trust that belongs to God alone. The principle in verse 18 applies in every age. Today, applying it does not mean mocking people of other faiths, which the psalm does not do, since it addresses the idols and the idol makers, not worshipers as persons. It means examining what has taken the place of the LORD in our own trust and noticing what it is making of us.

debates.question: Does verse 14 say the LORD will 'vindicate' His people or that He will 'judge' them?

views.label: He will vindicate them, a word of defence
views.case: In Deuteronomy 32:36 the context is God seeing 'that their strength is gone,' and then acting for them. Most English versions, the BSB included, follow that sense, and the second half of the verse, 'have compassion on His servants,' supports it.

views.label: He will judge them, a word of discipline and accountability
views.case: The Hebrew verb is the ordinary verb for judging, and the BSB footnote records that the Septuagint reads it that way. Hebrews 10:30 quotes the parallel in Deuteronomy as 'The Lord will judge His people,' as a warning.

views.label: Both, since the verb can carry both senses
views.case: Judging in Israel often meant putting things right for the wronged, as in the work of the judges, and the same verb can describe either side of that work. The verse then says that God will sort out His people's case, whichever way it goes.

debates.bearing: The compassion that follows, 'will have compassion on His servants,' keeps the verse from becoming either a threat or a mere comfort. God is both a defender and a judge, and He remains a God of mercy to His own.

debates.question: How does Psalm 135 relate to Psalm 115 and Jeremiah 10, and what does that say about its date?

views.label: It borrows from them, so it is later
views.case: The idol passage is clearly shorter and rearranged compared to Psalm 115, and the line in verse 7 sits in Jeremiah 10:13 in a context of mocking idols. Adding Levi to the list in verse 20 suggests a time when the Levites were prominent in the temple.

views.label: They draw on common liturgical material
views.case: Israel's hymnody may have used a stock of familiar lines for centuries, so that the same expressions appear in many places without any single dependence. On this reading the psalm may be earlier than it looks.

debates.bearing: The date does not change the meaning. In either case the psalm is the work of a person who treats earlier Scripture as living speech and arranges it for worship.

debates.question: Is the mockery of idols in verses 15 to 18 a fair account of what idol worshipers believed?

views.label: It is a deliberate caricature
views.case: Ancient peoples did not simply think their statue was the god. Many believed the deity was present in or through the image after the right rites, so the psalm targets the image on purpose to show the inadequacy of what is at the centre of worship.

views.label: It describes how the nations' trust works in practice
views.case: Whatever the theory, the image was made by craftsmen, kept in place, and carried about, as Jeremiah 10:5 says, 'They must be carried because they cannot walk.' The satire points to this plain fact.

debates.bearing: The aim of the psalm is not a study of other religions but a call to its own people. The sting is in verse 18, aimed at anyone who trusts in what cannot hear.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word in the psalm is the plural command halelu, 'praise,' and it is followed immediately by the name of God, Yah, short for Yahweh, so that 'Hallelujah' is literally 'praise the LORD,' and the BSB footnote says as much. The psalm is saturated with this word, in verses 1, 3 and 21. The verb halal carries the sense of boasting in, or celebrating, and to say 'hallelujah' is to make a joyful public noise about what the LORD is worth. The command is plural, which makes the whole psalm a corporate act.

Verse 3 contains a small ambiguity. 'Sing praises to His name, for it is lovely' can be read two ways in Hebrew. The word translated 'lovely' means pleasant, sweet or agreeable, and the Hebrew has no stated subject for it, so it can refer either to the name or to the act of singing. Is it the name that is pleasant, or is it pleasant to sing? Most translations choose the name. The best reading may be to leave both open, since the psalm treats praise as a delight rather than a duty.

In verse 5 the psalmist says, 'For I know that the LORD is great.' The Hebrew has the pronoun 'I' set beside the verb 'know,' so the sentence is emphatic, I myself know. This is the language of a person who has tested a claim and holds it as a conviction, and it contrasts with the idols whose makers 'do not comprehend or discern,' as Isaiah 44:18 says. The word 'our Lord,' adonenu, in the same verse shifts from the covenant name to the title of a master, and the claim is that this Master is 'above all gods.'

Verse 6 declares that the LORD 'does all that pleases Him.' The verb is chafets, to delight in or be pleased with, and the same line appears in Psalm 115:3. It is not a statement of whim. It is the delight of a God who is entirely free and whose pleasure is good, and the following verses show what that pleasure produces: rain, lightning, wind, rescue and a land for His people. In verse 7 the word for 'clouds' comes from the verb for lifting, so these are the things that are lifted up from the horizon, which matches Jeremiah 10:13, and the 'storehouses' of the wind are an image of God's reserves, a kind of weather treasury.

The idols in verse 15 are 'atsabbim, a word that is generally linked to a root for toil and hurt, and it appears in Psalm 115:4 as well. It may carry the sense of things made by painful labour. The verse says they are 'the work of the hands of men,' ma'aseh yedei adam. The contrast is with the LORD's own hands. The word for 'breath' in verse 17 is ruach, which is also the word for the wind in verse 7 and for spirit. The idols have no ruach, while the LORD brings forth the ruach from His storehouses. The same word marks the line between a dead thing and a living one.

Verse 14 uses the verb nacham in the reflexive form, yitnecham, which is commonly translated 'relent' or 'have compassion.' It carries the sense of a deep emotional turning, to be sorry or to be moved. The same verb is used of God in Exodus 32:14, when He relented from the disaster He had spoken of. The verb that precedes it, din, is the ordinary word for judge, which is why the footnote notes the alternative reading. The pair 'judge' and 'be moved to compassion' is the pair already found in Deuteronomy 32:36.

The last verse reverses the first: where verse 1 commands praise of the name, verse 21 says 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion,' with the passive participle barukh, a statement of fact that already carries the weight of a wish. The phrase 'He who dwells in Jerusalem,' shoken Yerushalayim, uses a verb that is related to the word for the divine presence, shekhinah, in later Jewish writing, and was connected from early on with the tabernacle, Exodus 25:8.

typology.type: The exodus and the defeat of Sihon and Og
typology.fulfillment: Verses 8 to 12 compress Israel's salvation into a single movement: a firstborn judgment, a rescue, and a land given. The New Testament sees the greater version of the pattern in Christ. At the Last Supper He gave the Passover new meaning, and at the cross He 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and 'made a public spectacle of them,' Colossians 2:15. The inheritance won is not a strip of land east of the Jordan but 'an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4. The type falls short because the conquest dealt with human kings and borders, while Christ deals with sin and death, and His victory is won by His own death, not by the sword.

Verse 4 echoes Exodus 19:5, where Israel is God's 'treasured possession' and, in the next verse, 'a kingdom of priests.' Peter applies those very words to a church drawn from every nation: 'a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9, and Paul says that Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession,' Titus 2:14. The escalation is that the people are no longer defined by descent from Jacob but by being united to Christ. The type falls short in that Israel was a single nation in a single land, while the new people are scattered among every nation and have no capital but the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22.

typology.type: The idols that have mouths but cannot speak
typology.fulfillment: The contrast between dead images and the living God is taken up in the New Testament in the person of Christ, who is called 'the Word' who 'became flesh,' John 1:14, and 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15. Where the idol is a human attempt to make God visible, Christ is God's own way of making Himself seen. Paul tells the Thessalonians how they 'turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,' 1 Thessalonians 1:9. The type falls short because the idols were only a negative picture, a list of what God is not, and Christ is the positive and complete answer, the One who speaks and sees and hears and gives breath.

study.christ:
Psalm 135 does not predict a person, but it asks a question that only Christ answers: how can a people who trust a living God have their trust vindicated in history? The psalm's answer is 'the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants,' verse 14. The New Testament says that this happened in a surprising way, through the death and resurrection of a servant who was Himself vindicated. Paul says that the Spirit 'vindicated' Him, 1 Timothy 3:16, and the cross which looked like the triumph of the powers turned out to be their defeat, Colossians 2:15. The exodus pattern, in which judgment falls on the oppressor and the people go free, finds its decisive form in Christ.

The psalm's contrast between dead idols and the living God also leads to Him. The idols have mouths that cannot speak, but the Word speaks. They have eyes that cannot see, but He looked at Peter and at the rich young man, and 'saw' the crowds, Mark 10:21, Matthew 9:36. They have ears that cannot hear, but He heard the cry of the blind man in a noisy crowd, Mark 10:47-49. They have no breath, but He breathed on His disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22. Where the psalm lists the senses that the dead gods lack, the Gospels record Christ using each of them for people in need.

The enduring name of verse 13 is another line to Christ. Exodus 3:15 gives the name as 'My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.' In Philippians 2:9-11 the name above every name is given to the Son, and every knee bows to confess that 'Jesus Christ is Lord.' The church is then given the task to 'proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light,' 1 Peter 2:9. The psalm's claim that God's name 'endures forever' becomes in the New Testament a claim about Jesus.

The warning of verse 18, that those who make idols become like them, also finds its reverse in Christ. Paul says that believers, 'with unveiled faces,' 'are being transformed into His image,' 2 Corinthians 3:18. The goal of worship, which is to become like the one worshiped, is reached for those who look to the living image of God rather than to a lifeless one. The Word does not leave His people deaf and mute. He opens deaf ears, Mark 7:34-35, and unstops mouths, so that the congregation can say 'Hallelujah' as the psalm demands. None of this turns the psalm's exodus or idol imagery into a code for Christ. It simply shows the lines on which the psalm, read with the rest of Scripture, runs to Him.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as free. 'The LORD does all that pleases Him,' verse 6, and the field of that freedom is the whole of reality: 'in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths.' It is a statement about God's sovereignty that is repeated with the opposite point in view in Psalm 115:3, where it answers the nations who ask, 'Where is their God?' God is not dependent on His creation, and no part of it, whether sky, sea or deep, lies outside what He can do. The sovereignty is made vivid by weather, a field in which humans see their own helplessness, with the LORD drawing clouds from the ends of the earth and keeping the wind in storehouses.

Second, the psalm shows a God who acts in history for a people He has chosen. Verse 4 gives the reason in a single phrase, 'the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own.' Deuteronomy 7:7-8 says that the choice was not because Israel was large, but because the LORD loved them and kept an oath. The psalm's tally of judgments, the firstborn, Pharaoh's servants, Sihon, Og, the kings of Canaan, is told in service of that love. It is hard to read verses 10 and 11 without feeling the weight of divine judgment, and the psalm does not apologise for it. It holds that God's faithfulness to His people sometimes involves opposing those who oppose them, a note the Bible sounds elsewhere, Exodus 34:7, and that the God of compassion is also the God of justice.

Third, the psalm shows God as the one who is alive. The list of dead organs in verses 16 and 17 is the foil for a God who sees, hears and speaks. The attributes shown here are relational ones: He knows His people, He remembers His name, He is moved with compassion, verse 14. The picture is not of a force or a principle, but of a personal being who can be addressed as 'You' in verse 13, and who dwells in Jerusalem in verse 21. That God dwells there does not shrink Him. Solomon knew that heaven could not contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27, and the psalm keeps both the cosmic view of verses 6 and 7 and the temple view of verse 21 in a single frame.

For worship, this means that praise is a response to something real, and the psalm asks the community to say so in the open. It also means that the God of Psalm 135 is the opposite of the objects people trust. They are made by human hands and need to be carried, Jeremiah 10:5. He carries His people. They have no breath. He is the source of the wind. Those who 'fear the LORD,' verse 20, are not the frightened but those who give Him the weight the psalm has described, and who find, as the psalmist did, that the God who is far above all gods is the one who 'will have compassion on His servants.'

crossReferences.note: The source of the idol passage. Psalm 115 lists more things the idols lack, noses, hands and feet, and Psalm 135 shortens the list to end on 'no breath.' Reading them together shows how one psalm adapts another to its own argument, and that verse 18 is the shared punchline, 'Those who make them become like them.'

The line about the clouds and the storehouses of the wind appears here almost verbatim, set against mockery of idols made of wood. The setting shows why the psalm includes it: the God who runs the weather is set against objects that have to be nailed in place.

Verse 36 supplies the two key verbs of Psalm 135:14, judge or vindicate and have compassion. It comes from the Song of Moses, where God sees that Israel's strength is gone and steps in, which gives the psalm's confidence a covenant foundation.

The treasured possession of verse 4 comes from here, from the opening of the covenant at Sinai. Israel's status rests on God's whole-earth ownership, 'for the whole earth is Mine,' which is why the psalm can say both that He chose Jacob and that He rules all creation.

The story of Sihon and Og, whose defeat the psalm lists in verses 10 and 11. The account shows that Sihon refused passage and attacked first, and it explains why these two kings became fixed symbols of what God did on Israel's behalf.

A long satire on the craftsman who burns half a tree to warm himself and bows to the other half. It expands Psalm 135:15-18 into a story, with the same conclusion, that the person who trusts such an object 'cannot deliver himself.'

Quotes Deuteronomy 32:36 as 'The Lord will judge His people,' which is the reading flagged in the BSB footnote on Psalm 135:14. It shows that the verse was heard in the early church as a sober word to the people of God, not only as a comfort.

Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities' at the cross. It is the New Testament's answer to the exodus and conquest verses of the psalm, now won not against Pharaoh or Og but against every power that held people captive.

Takes the language of the 'treasured possession' from Exodus 19 and the psalm and applies it to the church: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a people for God's own possession. The reason given is the psalm's own purpose, to 'proclaim the virtues' of the One who called them.

A great multitude in heaven cries 'Hallelujah' and praises God's true and just judgments, then a voice says 'Praise our God, all you who serve Him.' It is the same shape as Psalm 135, praise rooted in God's judgments, and the call to all servants to join.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 135 answers a question that the story of Scripture raises from its first chapters: whose world is this, and who is really in charge of it? Genesis 1 says it is the world of one God, who made the heavens and the earth, and Psalm 135 reads that claim in the language of weather and war. The same God who sends rain and lightning, verse 7, is the God who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, verse 8. Creation and redemption are not two stories but one. The Creator is the Redeemer, and the world He made is the world He is rescuing a people in.

It also answers the fall's long shadow. Genesis 3 begins when the human race trusts a voice other than God's, and Romans 1:23 describes how that turned into the worship of images. Psalm 135:15-18 is a compact diagnosis of the result. The nations are not simply mistaken; they have trusted in things that cannot hear, and they have been shaped by what they trusted. The psalm tells a story of how God breaks into that condition by choosing 'Jacob as His own' and giving him a land and a law, so that there would be at least one people in the world who knew the difference between the living God and the made one.

Looking ahead, the psalm points to the promise that God's choice of one people was always for the sake of all. Israel was God's treasured possession in order to be 'a kingdom of priests,' Exodus 19:6, and the priestly vocation was to bless the nations, Genesis 12:3. In Christ the people widen to include those from every nation, and the descriptions of Israel in verse 4 are applied to the church, 1 Peter 2:9. The conquest of Canaan and the defeat of Egypt find their meaning in the greater rescue of the cross, Colossians 2:15, and the inheritance of the land becomes the inheritance of the whole world, Romans 4:13, and the kingdom of heaven, 1 Peter 1:4.

The story ends where the psalm ends, in a great congregation blessing God. In Revelation 19 the shout of 'Hallelujah' goes up from a multitude 'like the rushing of many waters' because 'the Lord our God the Almighty reigns,' Revelation 19:6. The idols are gone, along with the Babylon that made them, and what remains is the living God dwelling with His people, with no temple needed, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The psalm's final cry, 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem,' is then fully true, for the new Jerusalem is where He dwells, and the whole creation speaks.

quiz.q: According to verse 4, why has the LORD chosen Jacob?

options.text: Because Israel is His treasured possession.
options.note: Verse 4 states this directly, echoing Exodus 19:5's language of chosen belonging.

options.text: Because Israel was the strongest nation on earth.
options.note: The psalm never grounds God's choice in Israel's strength or merit.

options.text: Because Israel had no idols at the time.
options.note: The psalm does not give this as the reason for God's choice; it simply names Israel as His treasured possession.

options.text: Because Jacob built the first temple.
options.note: Solomon, not Jacob, built the first temple; this is not the psalm's stated reason.

quiz.q: What specific historical acts does the psalm recall as proof of God's power?

options.text: Striking Egypt's firstborn and defeating Sihon, Og, and the kings of Canaan.
options.note: Verses 8-12 name exactly these events as proof of the LORD's sovereign power in history.

options.text: The building of Solomon's temple.
options.note: The temple's construction is not mentioned in this psalm's historical recital.

options.text: The return from the Babylonian exile.
options.note: While the psalm may date from the post exilic period, the events it recounts are the exodus and conquest, not the return itself.

options.text: The crossing of the Jordan under Joshua alone.
options.note: The psalm's specific historical recital centers on Egypt's plagues and the defeat of named kings, not the Jordan crossing.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the idols of the nations?

options.text: Silver and gold, made by human hands, unable to speak, see, or hear.
options.note: Verses 15-17 describe idols in exactly these terms, mocking their powerlessness.

options.text: Powerful spirits that rival the LORD's authority.
options.note: The psalm insists idols have no real power at all, unlike this option suggests.

options.text: Ancient relics no longer worshiped by anyone.
options.note: The psalm addresses idols as actively worshiped and trusted, not as forgotten relics.

options.text: Living creatures created by the LORD for a purpose.
options.note: Idols are described as lifeless objects made by human hands, not living creatures.

quiz.q: What warning does verse 18 give about those who trust in idols?

options.text: They become like the idols they trust, lifeless and unresponsive.
options.note: Verse 18 states this directly: those who make and trust idols become like them.

options.text: They will immediately lose all their possessions.
options.note: The psalm's warning is about spiritual likeness to idols, not material loss specifically.

options.text: They will be physically struck down like Egypt's firstborn.
options.note: That judgment is described earlier in the psalm concerning Egypt, but verse 18's warning is about becoming like lifeless idols.

options.text: Nothing; the psalm gives no consequence for idol worship.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly states a serious spiritual consequence.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up this psalm's theme of the living God versus lifeless idols?

options.text: Christ, the living Word, defeats hostile powers and is given the name above every name.
options.note: Colossians 2:15 and Philippians 2:9-11 develop exactly this contrast between Christ's living power and the powerlessness this psalm ascribes to idols.

options.text: The New Testament abandons any concern with idolatry.
options.note: The New Testament repeatedly warns against idolatry, continuing this psalm's concern.

options.text: It applies this theme only to first century Roman emperor worship.
options.note: The New Testament's warnings against idolatry are broader than one historical instance.

options.text: It reverses the psalm's teaching, treating idols as equally valid paths to God.
options.note: The New Testament, like this psalm, insists idols are powerless and unworthy of trust, not equally valid.

questions: The psalm calls Israel God's 'treasured possession.' How does knowing you are treasured by God, not merely tolerated, change the way you approach Him in prayer this week?
Verses 8-12 root praise in specific, remembered acts of God in history. What specific things has God actually done in your own life that you could recount today as grounds for praise?
The psalm mocks idols that have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see. What modern 'idols,' things you look to for security or identity, might be just as powerless as the psalm describes?
Verse 18 warns that those who trust idols become like them, lifeless. Where might you be shaping your own heart after something that cannot truly see, hear, or save you?

The psalm ends with every house, Israel, Aaron, Levi, and 'all who fear the LORD,' called to bless Him together. Who could you invite into worship with you this week who might otherwise praise God alone?

translationNotes.note: Treasured possession renders segullah, a term for private, especially valued property, used of Israel also in Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6.
Vindicate can also be rendered judge, reflecting a Hebrew verb that covers both defending the innocent and rendering righteous verdicts.
This description of idols closely parallels Psalm 115:4-8, suggesting a shared liturgical tradition mocking idol worship across multiple psalms.
